Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans from new patients. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-scans-only approach for automatically detecting

Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and

at multiple stages of a process, determined by event quantities and case
completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior under
different process conditions. Our experiments surprisingly reveal that the basic
Multi-layer Perceptron frequently surpasses more advanced deep learning models
in both prediction tasks. Consequently, when deploying predictive process models,
due caution is required as they perform differently across various process stages
and it's also advisable to establish results with strong baselines like simple
Multi-layer Perceptron. Our findings also imply that predicting the duration of
process cases is significantly more challenging than the preceding event
characteristics and occurrence time. Furthermore, we found that process stages
with low event counts pose a higher predictive difficulty for both event
characteristics and occurrence time than stages with high event counts. Our
data, employed to train the models, includes 9 publicly available process datasets

This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. Another screen is more distant, estimated to be around 8.8 parsecs from the Earth, and is associated with a distinct structure within the Local Bubble known as the Castano Cloud. The data also reveal the effects of this more distant screen on the scintillation patterns, revealing patterns that shift and change over a 5.7-year period and are influenced by the position of the screen and the pulsar relative to the solar system's barycentric coordinates. The interactions between this screen and the nearby void and cloud can result in varying levels of scattering that lead to the degradation of the signal of the pulsar. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. This paper also provides a scalable LGCN framework through a computationally efficient approximation of hyperbolic graph operations. Experimental results show that LGCN outperforms regular GCNs by an average 6.6% in terms of accuracy. This approach has the potential to be applied to various applications that rely on Euclidean distances, such as graph classification, node classification, and link prediction. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. This research paves the way for innovative medical imaging applications and showcases the practical usage of medical GANs in disease-aware image editing. This research has significant implications for the usage of AI in the healthcare field and could potentially be applied to various medical conditions across different imaging modalities.
